sources.note: The ASCII file header names NASA/TP-2008-214170 (dated 2008 Oct 07), whereas the NASA publication page https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/SEpubs/5MKSE.html names NASA/TP-2009-214174 (published 2009 January). The errata page https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/5MCSE/5MKSEerrata.html notes that tabulated values of delta T and longitude on pages A-56 to A-150 were incorrect in the hard copy only and corrected in the PDF. Sun coordinates use VSOP87 (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988) and Moon coordinates use ELP-2000/82 (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983) with lunar secular acceleration n-dot = -25.858 arcsec/cy^2 (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002). The largest uncertainty in the eclipse predictions is fluctuations in Earth's rotation expressed as delta T: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records by Morrison and Stephenson (2004), 1955-present from published observations, and future values extrapolated from the long-term tidal trend.

sources.note: Earth's penumbral and umbral shadow sizes are calculated with Danjon's enlargement method; Sun and Moon coordinates use VSOP87 and ELP-2000/82 with n-dot = -25.858 arcsec/cy^2. Where the catalog key lists '*' for a total penumbral lunar eclipse, the ASCII catalog file writes 'x' (141 rows, all with penumbral magnitude >= 1). As for solar eclipses, the largest uncertainty is delta T: pre-1950s from Morrison and Stephenson (2004), 1955-2006 from published observations, and post-2006 extrapolated from the tidal trend.

files.note: All 11,898 solar eclipses from -1999 to +3000 across all 21 columns of 5MKSEcatalog.txt, with evidenceClass 'predicted'. Dates use the Julian calendar through 1582 October 4 and the Gregorian calendar from 1582 October 15, with astronomical year numbering (year 0 = 1 BCE).

All 12,064 lunar eclipses from -1999 to +3000 across all 20 columns of 5MKLEcatalog.txt, with evidenceClass 'predicted'. Dates use the Julian calendar through 1582 October 4 and the Gregorian calendar from 1582 October 15, with astronomical year numbering (year 0 = 1 BCE).
